reading.body:
Crane DC - Portland publishes 36,000 square feet of technical space but no megawatt figure, making it impossible to estimate compute capacity or AI suitability from the data available.

Power capacity is the irreducible requirement for assessing any data center's role in AI infrastructure scaling. The facility's technical footprint could support anything from modest enterprise workloads to substantial training clusters depending on electrical delivery, cooling systems, and structural load capacity, none of which are disclosed. This opacity is typical across Oregon, where 133 mapped facilities exist but only six have published any megawatt specification at all, totaling 182 MW across the entire state.

The seven certifications on record, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, FISMA, NIST 800-53, HITRUST, SSAE 18, and LEED, indicate a compliance posture oriented toward regulated financial, healthcare, and federal workloads rather than the high-density compute clusters that AI training requires. These certifications do not disqualify a facility from supporting AI infrastructure, but they do not indicate it either. Without published power and cooling specifications, the facility remains invisible to any analysis of grid-constrained AI scaling.
